summary: The Jaecoo J5 EV is the battery-electric member of Chery's Jaecoo J5 small-SUV line, sold in Australia in a single fully-loaded EV Summit grade alongside separate petrol and hybrid J5s that share the body but not the drivetrain. Australian reviewers rate it as one of the cheapest ways into a well-equipped electric SUV, praising the 130kW DC charging, the eight-year warranty and a $1,520 eight-year servicing bill, while splitting over how it drives: Chasing Cars found the ride absorbent where others called it sharp, and most criticise the steering, brake feel and throttle calibration. Testers saw real-world consumption between about 14.7 and 17.5kWh/100km, which puts genuine range nearer 340-350km than the 399km WLTP figure for the UK-market twin on the same pack and 18-inch tyres.
pros: Cheapest end of the electric small-SUV class at Jaecoo's own recommended retail price of $35,990 before on-road costs, and a $36,990 national drive-away offer has been rolled over since launch (the current one runs to 30 November 2026), about $1,400 under the roughly $38,400 Victorian drive-away the list price implies
Novated-lease buyers get a standing 10% national fleet discount off the $35,990 recommended retail price through an approved fleet management organisation, on top of the BEV FBT exemption
130kW DC peak charging (30-80% in about 28 minutes) and 10.3kW three-phase AC, both well ahead of the 80kW-class Chery E5 it shares a 58.9kWh-usable LFP pack with

Eight-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle and high-voltage battery warranty, conditional only on servicing to the manufacturer's schedule, with eight years of capped-price servicing totalling $1,520; roadside assistance also runs to eight years but only if renewed at each scheduled service at an authorised Jaecoo dealer
Rated to tow 1,250kg braked on the manufacturer's own spec sheet, against the 750kg of most cheap Chinese electric SUVs including the Chery E5, BYD Atto 2 and GWM Ora 5
cons: Real-world consumption well above the rating: CarExpert saw 14.7kWh/100km, Chasing Cars 17.5kWh/100km and a 337km real-world range, against 399km WLTP

Front-drive chassis is unresolved: reviewers report very light steering with little self-centring, a squishy brake pedal with weak regeneration, an abrupt throttle at 60-80km/h and, on some test cars, torque steer under moderate throttle
Ride divides reviewers (absorbent to Chasing Cars, sharp over coarse bitumen to others), and the 235/55 R18 tyres carry a repair kit rather than a spare, where the closely related Chery E5 gets one
No ANCAP rating: reviewers at launch reported it untested, unlike the BYD Atto 2 and Kia EV3 it is cross-shopped against
Jaecoo is a 2025-vintage nameplate in Australia with no resale, parts or reliability record, and rolling drive-away campaigns work against used values
